title: The Role of Magnets in Navigation and Daily Life
content: Reshma lives in a coastal town of Kerala and is very fond of writing short stories. Her grandmother loves listening to her stories, so Reshma was writing a new story to share with her grandmother on her 60th birthday. Exploring Magnets The story was based on a ship carrying spices from Kerala for trade in the olden days. Reshma was aware that in those days, the sailors used stars to find directions at night. But in her story, a situation arose wherein the sailors got caught in a storm with an overcast sky and stars were not visible. Reshma could not take her story forward as she could not think of a way for sailors to find directions. She searched for in formation on the in ternet and her school library. She learnt that the travellers used a device, known as a magnetic compass, for finding directions. Reshma had seen pencil boxes and purses which had magnets to keep them closed. A writing board in her school also had a duster with a magnet. But she had never looked at those carefully. She now became curious to learn more about magnets and magnetic compasses.
learning_objective: Understand the historical use of magnets for navigation and identify their presence in common household items.
summary: Historically, magnets were crucial for navigation, as seen with the magnetic compass used by sailors. Today, magnets are found in many everyday objects like pencil boxes and writing boards.
subtopic_title: The Discovery and Everyday Use of Magnets

title: Distinguishing Natural and Artificial Magnets
content: The magnets used by sailors in the olden days were based on naturally occurring magnets, known as lodestones which were discovered in ancient times. Later on, people found out that magnets could also be made from pieces of iron. Nowadays, we have magnets made of different materials. The magnets that you find in your school laboratory and those used in pencil boxes, stickers, toys are all artificial magnets.
learning_objective: Differentiate between naturally occurring magnets (lodestones) and modern artificial magnets, understanding their origin and common applications.
summary: Natural magnets, called lodestones, were discovered in ancient times. Today, most magnets are artificial, made from materials like iron, and are found in many everyday items such as toys and school supplies.
subtopic_title: Natural and Artificial Magnets and Their Shapes

title: Identifying Different Shapes of Magnets
content: The magnets can be of various shapes. Common examples include Bar magnet, U-shaped magnet, and Ring magnet.
learning_objective: Identify and recognize common shapes of artificial magnets, such as bar, U-shaped, and ring magnets.
summary: Artificial magnets come in many forms, with common examples including the bar magnet, U-shaped magnet, and ring magnet.
subtopic_title: Natural and Artificial Magnets and Their Shapes

title: Activity: Classifying Materials by Magnetic Attraction
content: Collect a few objects made of different materials and also a magnet. Predict which of the objects will stick to the magnet. Now hold a magnet in your hand and bring it near the objects one by one. Observe which of the objects stick to the magnet. Do magnets stick to objects made of certain materials only? Record your observations. Was your prediction correct for all objects? Which materials stuck to the magnet? What conclusion can you draw?
learning_objective: Conduct a simple experiment to observe which objects are attracted to a magnet and make predictions about their magnetic properties.
summary: Perform an experiment by bringing a magnet close to various objects to observe which ones are attracted. This helps identify materials that interact with magnets.
subtopic_title: Identifying Materials Attracted by a Magnet (Activity 4.1)

title: Understanding Magnetic Materials
content: Through this activity, we found out that some of the objects were attracted to the magnet and stuck to it, while others were not. The materials which are attracted towards a magnet are called magnetic materials. The metal iron is a magnetic material. Nickel and cobalt are other metals that are also magnetic. Some of their combinations with other metals are also attracted towards magnets.
learning_objective: Define magnetic materials and identify common examples such as iron, nickel, and cobalt.
summary: Magnetic materials are substances attracted to a magnet. Key examples include metals like iron, nickel, and cobalt, and some of their alloys.
subtopic_title: Identifying Materials Attracted by a Magnet (Activity 4.1)

title: Understanding Non-magnetic Materials
content: The materials which are not attracted towards a magnet are called non-magnetic materials. Which materials listed in Table 4.1 were found to be non-magnetic?
learning_objective: Define non-magnetic materials and identify examples of materials that are not attracted to a magnet.
summary: Non-magnetic materials are those that are not attracted by a magnet, such as wood, plastic, or glass.
subtopic_title: Identifying Materials Attracted by a Magnet (Activity 4.1)

title: Demonstrating Magnetic Poles Using Iron Filings
content: Spread some iron filings (very small pieces of iron) on a sheet of paper. Place a bar magnet over them. Tap the paper and observe carefully what happens to the iron filings. Do you observe anything special about the way they stick to the magnet? Do the iron filings stick all over the magnet uniformly? Or do the iron filings stick more at some places? We find that maximum iron filings stick near the ends of the bar magnet, while a very few iron filings stick at the remaining part of the magnet. Do all parts of a magnet attract magnetic materials equally? If we repeat this activity with magnets of other shapes, do we get the same result?
learning_objective: Perform an activity to observe that magnetic attraction is strongest at specific points on a magnet, leading to the identification of poles.
summary: An experiment with iron filings demonstrates that a magnet's attractive force is concentrated at its ends, indicating the location of its poles, and not uniformly distributed.

title: Identifying the North and South Poles of a Magnet
content: These ends of the magnet are called the two poles of the magnet—the North pole and the South pole. Most of the iron filings stick to the poles of a magnet of any shape.
learning_objective: Define the North and South poles as the regions of strongest magnetic attraction on a magnet.
summary: The two ends of a magnet, where magnetic attraction is strongest, are known as the North pole and the South pole.

title: Magnets Always Have Two Poles
content: It is not possible to obtain a magnet with a single pole. If a magnet is broken into smaller pieces, North and South poles always exist in pairs even in the smallest piece of the magnet. A single North pole or a South pole cannot exist.
learning_objective: Understand and explain the fundamental principle that magnetic poles always exist in pairs (North and South) and cannot be isolated.
summary: A magnet always has both a North and a South pole; even if broken into smaller pieces, each new piece will still possess both poles, as a single isolated pole cannot exist.

title: Activity: Observing the Directional Property of a Suspended Magnet
content: Suspend a bar magnet with a thread tied to the middle of the magnet. You may need to adjust the position of the string till the magnet is balanced horizontally. Now rotate the magnet gently in the horizontal direction and let it come to rest. Mark the position corresponding to the ends of the magnet on the ground. Join these two points on the ground with a line. This line indicates the direction along which the magnet comes to rest. Now again rotate the magnet by giving a gentle push at its one end and wait till it comes to rest. Does the magnet rest along the same line?
learning_objective: Perform an experiment to observe that a freely suspended bar magnet consistently aligns itself in a specific direction.
summary: By suspending a bar magnet freely and rotating it, one can observe that it consistently returns to rest aligned along a particular direction, demonstrating its directional property.

title: Understanding North-South Alignment and Earth as a Magnet
content: A freely suspended magnet comes to rest along the north-south direction. The end of the magnet that points towards north direction is called the North-seeking pole or the North pole of the magnet. The other end that points towards the South direction is called the South-seeking pole or the South pole of the magnet. A freely suspended magnet rests along the north-south direction because our Earth itself behaves like a giant magnet.
learning_objective: Explain why a freely suspended magnet aligns itself in the North-South direction and relate this to Earth's magnetic properties.
summary: A freely suspended magnet consistently points North-South, with its ends defined as North-seeking and South-seeking poles. This phenomenon occurs because Earth itself acts as a massive magnet.

title: Using Magnetic Alignment to Identify Magnets
content: Repeat this activity with a small iron bar in place of the bar magnet. What do you observe? Does it always rest along north-south direction? It does not. It can rest along any direction. This implies that only magnets rest along north-south direction. This activity provides us with a way to test whether a piece of metal is a magnet or not.
learning_objective: Use the directional property of a freely suspended magnet to distinguish between magnetic and non-magnetic materials.
summary: Only true magnets consistently align themselves North-South when freely suspended. This property can be used to test whether an unknown piece of metal is a magnet or not, as non-magnetic materials will not show this alignment.

title: The Magnetic Compass: A Tool for Direction Finding
content: The property of a freely suspended magnet to always rest along the north-south direction is used to find directions. Based on this, a small device called a magnetic compass was developed in olden days for finding directions. It has a magnet in the shape of a needle which can rotate freely. The needle of a magnetic compass indicates the north-south direction.
learning_objective: Explain the primary purpose of a magnetic compass and how its freely rotating magnetic needle indicates the North-South direction.
summary: A magnetic compass is a navigation tool that utilizes a freely rotating magnetic needle, which always aligns itself in the North-South direction, to help find directions.

title: Using a Magnetic Compass to Determine Directions
content: The compass is kept at the place where we wish to know the directions. After some time, the needle comes to rest in the north-south direction. The compass box is then gently rotated until the north and south marked on the dial are aligned with the needle. Now all directions at that place are as indicated on the dial.
learning_objective: Describe the steps involved in using a magnetic compass to accurately determine all cardinal directions.
summary: To use a magnetic compass, place it on a flat surface, wait for the needle to settle North-South, then rotate the compass box until the dial's North and South markings match the needle, revealing all directions.

title: Components and Design of a Magnetic Compass
content: A magnetic compass is usually a small circular box with a transparent cover on it. The magnet, in the shape of a needle, is mounted on a pin standing on the bottom of the box. This needle is balanced on the pin in such a manner that it can move around this point easily, that is, it can rotate freely. The end of the needle which rests in the North direction is usually painted red. Below the needle, there is a dial with directions marked on it.
learning_objective: Identify and describe the key components of a magnetic compass, including its needle, pivot, and dial.
summary: A magnetic compass typically consists of a small circular box with a transparent cover, a freely rotating magnetic needle mounted on a pin, and a dial marked with directions beneath the needle.

title: How to Magnetize an Iron Needle
content: Collect a few materials like a cork piece, iron sewing needle, a permanent bar magnet, a glass bowl, and water. Place the iron sewing needle on a wooden table. Then keep any one pole of the magnet at one end of the needle. Move the magnet over the needle along its length. When it reaches the other end of the needle, lift it up. Bring the same pole of the magnet you started with to the same end of the sewing needle from which you began, and repeat the previous step. Repeat this process at least 30 to 40 times. Bring some iron filings or steel pins near the needle. If the pins or iron filings get attracted to the needle, then that means that the needle has become a magnet.
learning_objective: Follow instructions to magnetize an iron sewing needle using a permanent bar magnet, and test its magnetism.
summary: An iron needle can be magnetized by repeatedly stroking it in one direction with a permanent magnet. Its successful magnetization can be verified by its ability to attract small iron filings or pins.

title: Building a Simple Magnetic Compass
content: Pass this needle through the cork horizontally. Float the cork in a glass bowl filled with water, such that the needle always remains above the level of water. When the needle comes to rest, your magnetic compass is ready for use. Note the direction in which either side of the needle points. Rotate the cork gently and wait till it stops rotating. Repeat this a few more times. Do the ends of the needle always point in the same direction?
learning_objective: Construct a functional, simple magnetic compass using a magnetized needle, a cork, and a bowl of water, and observe its directional behavior.
summary: A simple magnetic compass can be built by embedding a magnetized needle into a cork and floating it in water. The needle will align itself North-South, indicating directions.

title: Ancient Indian Navigation: The Matsya-Yantra
content: Much before the widespread use of the modern magnetic compass, a device similar to the compass needle made by you was used by Indians for navigation at sea. It consisted of a magnetised fish-shaped iron piece, kept in a vessel of oil. It was called matsya-yantra (or machchhyantra).
learning_objective: Appreciate the historical development of navigation tools by learning about the ancient Indian matsya-yantra.
summary: Before modern compasses, ancient Indians used the 'matsya-yantra,' a magnetized fish-shaped iron piece floating in oil, for sea navigation.

title: Observing Attraction and Repulsion Between Magnets
content: Take a pair of bar magnets on which North and South poles have been marked. Place the longer side of magnet A over 5–6 round shaped pencils. Now bring one end of magnet B near the end of magnet A placed on the pencils. Make sure that the two magnets do not touch each other. Observe what happens. Next, bring the other end of magnet B near the same end of magnet A. Does the magnet A on the pencils begin to move? Does it always move in the direction of the approaching magnet? What do these observations suggest?
learning_objective: Conduct an experiment to directly observe the forces of attraction and repulsion when bringing different poles of two bar magnets close to each other.
summary: By bringing marked bar magnets together, one can observe that some interactions cause the magnets to attract, while others cause them to repel, demonstrating fundamental magnetic forces.

title: Understanding the Laws of Magnetic Attraction and Repulsion
content: You will see that unlike poles of two magnets, that is, the North pole of one magnet and the South pole of another magnet, attract each other. The like poles, that is, either the North poles or the South poles of both magnets, repel each other.
learning_objective: State the fundamental law of magnetism: unlike poles attract, and like poles repel.
summary: The fundamental rule of magnetism states that opposite poles (North and South) attract each other, while similar poles (North-North or South-South) repel each other.

title: Distinguishing Magnets from Iron Using Repulsion
content: Repeat the activity by using an iron bar in place of one of the magnets. What do you observe this time? You will find that both the ends of the iron bar will be attracted by both the North and South poles of the magnet. From this activity, we find that a magnet can be identified by its property of repulsion.
learning_objective: Explain how an iron bar is attracted by both poles of a magnet, and conclude that only repulsion can definitively identify a magnet.
summary: An iron bar is attracted by both poles of a magnet, but only a true magnet will experience repulsion from another magnet's like pole. Therefore, repulsion is the definitive test to identify a magnet.

title: Observing Compass Needle Deflection with a Bar Magnet
content: Take a magnetic compass and a bar magnet. Place the magnetic compass over a horizontal surface and wait for its needle to come to rest. Now slowly bring North pole of the bar magnet close to the North pole of the compass needle. Observe the compass needle carefully. What do you observe? Does the needle deflect? If yes, in which direction? Now repeat the above step with the South pole of the bar magnet. Do you observe any difference this time? The compass needle is also a magnet. Will it show the same behaviour if a magnet is brought closer to it?
learning_objective: Perform an experiment to observe how the magnetic needle of a compass deflects when a bar magnet is brought near, applying the concepts of attraction and repulsion.
summary: Observe the deflection of a magnetic compass needle when a bar magnet's North or South pole is brought near. This demonstrates the forces of attraction and repulsion between magnets.

title: Analyzing Compass Deflection: Like Poles Repel, Unlike Poles Attract
content: When the North pole of a magnet is brought closer to the North pole of the compass needle, it moves away. When the South pole of the magnet is brought closer to the North pole of the compass needle, it moves closer.
learning_objective: Explain the observed deflections of a compass needle by applying the rules of magnetic attraction (unlike poles) and repulsion (like poles).
summary: Bringing a magnet's North pole near a compass needle's North pole causes repulsion, while bringing its South pole causes attraction, illustrating the fundamental magnetic principles.

title: Investigating Magnetic Force Through Non-Magnetic Barriers
content: Repeat the first or second part of Activity 4.6. Without disturbing the bar magnet and magnetic compass, place a piece of wood between them, perpendicular to the table. Observe the compass needle carefully. Is there any effect on the deflection of compass needle due to the piece of wood? Repeat the process by replacing the piece of wood with a cardboard sheet, thin plastic sheet, and a thin glass sheet. Suppose we place a piece of wood between the compass needle and the magnet. Will this affect the deflection of the compass needle?
learning_objective: Conduct an experiment to determine if non-magnetic materials placed between a magnet and a compass needle affect the magnetic interaction.
summary: Perform an experiment by placing various non-magnetic materials (wood, cardboard, plastic, glass) between a magnet and a compass to observe if they block or alter the magnetic effect.

title: Magnetic Force Penetrates Non-Magnetic Barriers
content: You would observe that there is no appreciable change in the deflection of the needle when a sheet of any of the above material is placed between the magnet and the compass needle. Therefore, we can conclude that the magnetic effect can act through non-magnetic materials.
learning_objective: Conclude from experimental observations that magnetic forces can pass through non-magnetic materials without significant reduction.
summary: Experiments show that non-magnetic materials like wood or plastic do not obstruct magnetic forces, indicating that magnetic effects can pass through them.

title: Exploring Magnetic Properties Through Fun Activities
content: After learning about magnets, Reshma was excited and decided to set up some fun activities using magnets at her school fair. You may try making these yourself and may also think of some more fun ideas. Magnets can move some objects without touching them! Is that not amazing? Can we make a garland? Can we take the steel balls out of the maze by moving a magnet below the cardboard tray? Can we pick out a steel paper clip fallen in water using a magnet, without getting our fingers or the magnet wet? Will two matchbox-magnet cars with like poles facing each other speed towards each other or run away from each other when brought closer?
learning_objective: Engage in various hands-on activities to observe how magnets can interact with objects at a distance and apply knowledge of attraction/repulsion in playful scenarios.
summary: Explore the fascinating properties of magnets through various fun activities like creating magnetic garlands, navigating steel balls through a maze, picking up objects from water, and predicting the interaction of magnet-powered cars.

title: How to Prevent Magnets from Losing Their Strength
content: "Do not heat me or drop me or hammer me. Do not keep me near mobile phones or remote controls." Caution Have fun, but treat magnets with care.
learning_objective: Identify common actions, such as heating, dropping, or exposing to electronic devices, that can cause a magnet to lose its magnetic properties.
summary: To maintain a magnet's strength, avoid heating, dropping, or hammering it, and keep it away from electronic devices like mobile phones and remote controls.

title: Best Practices for Storing Magnets
content: How to keep the magnets safe? Magnet says, "Store me properly. Keep me in pairs with unlike poles on the same side. Keep a piece of wood in between. Place two pieces of soft iron across the ends." N S S Wooden piece Iron piece
learning_objective: Describe the recommended methods for storing magnets, including pairing them with unlike poles and using soft iron pieces, to preserve their magnetic strength.
summary: Proper magnet storage involves keeping them in pairs with unlike poles together, separated by a piece of wood, and placing soft iron pieces across their ends to maintain their magnetic strength.
